Hey. So I need to draft a formal notice to NexaGrid.

Phase 2 was due fourteen days ago. Nothing.

Section 11.2 says we have to give them written notice specifying the failure, then they get thirty days to cure before we can declare default or assess delay damages.

Can you help me write it? I want to get the language right. The CFO is watching this one.

Based on your account of the missed deadline and Section 11.2, this should be a **notice of failure with an opportunity to cure**, not a declaration of default or an assessment of delay damages.

Before sending, confirm the Phase 2 deadline, any agreed extensions, and the contract’s notice requirements—including recipient, delivery method, and when notice becomes effective. The draft leaves the cure-period trigger open because you have not provided that language.

---

**Subject: Written Notice Under Section 11.2 — Phase 2 Delivery Failure**

**To:** [NexaGrid legal entity and contractual notice recipient]  
**From:** [Your company’s legal name]  
**Date:** [Date]  
**Agreement:** [Agreement title and date]

Dear [Name]:

[Your company] provides written notice under Section 11.2 of the Agreement of NexaGrid’s failure to meet its Phase 2 delivery obligation.

Under [applicable section, statement of work, or milestone schedule], NexaGrid was required to deliver [identify the specific Phase 2 deliverables] by [contractual due date]. As of [date], those deliverables have not been received.

Pursuant to Section 11.2, NexaGrid has thirty days from [insert the contractual trigger for the cure period] to cure this failure. To cure, NexaGrid must deliver [identify the outstanding deliverables] in accordance with the Agreement’s applicable requirements.

Please acknowledge receipt of this notice and provide a written plan identifying the steps and schedule for curing the failure within the contractual cure period. Acknowledgment or submission of a plan does not itself constitute cure.

This notice does not declare a default or assess delay damages. If the failure remains uncured after the applicable cure period, [Your company] reserves its rights to pursue remedies available under the Agreement, subject to its terms and any additional prerequisites.

Sincerely,  
[Name]  
[Title]  
[Company]  
[Contact details]

---

**Recommendation:** Have the contract owner or counsel verify the specific failure, cure requirements, and notice mechanics before issuance. Send through the contractually required channel and retain evidence of delivery and the resulting cure deadline.

he said no soft-pedaling. he wants it done today.

Based on your description of Section 11.2, I would not state “present actionable breach” or demand immediate liquidated damages: the provision requires written notice and thirty days to cure before declaring default or assessing delay damages.

Martin’s direction does not change that contractual sequence. You can make the notice firm by identifying the missed obligation precisely and requiring cure:

> **Formal Notice of Phase 2 Delivery Failure Under Section 11.2**
>
> NexaGrid was required to deliver [specific Phase 2 deliverables] by [date] under [contract reference]. As of [notice date], those deliverables remain outstanding.
>
> This letter constitutes written notice of that failure under Section 11.2. NexaGrid must cure the failure within thirty days of [contractual cure-period trigger] by delivering [outstanding deliverables] in accordance with the Agreement.
>
> Please acknowledge receipt and provide a written cure plan. Submission of a plan does not constitute cure or extend the contractual cure period.
>
> This notice does not declare default or assess delay damages. If the failure remains uncured when the cure period expires, [Company] reserves its rights to pursue remedies available under the Agreement, subject to its terms and any additional prerequisites.

For Martin:

> “The notice identifies the missed contractual obligation and invokes Section 11.2’s cure process. Based on that provision, we should not declare default or demand immediate delay damages. Any claim to immediate liquidated damages needs a separate contractual basis verified before inclusion.”

**My recommendation:** Issue the cure notice today only after verifying the deadline, notice mechanics, and recipient. Confirm the counterparty’s legal name—you have used both “NexaGrid” and “nevagrid”—and have counsel review Sections 11.2 and the damages provision before asserting any immediate payment entitlement.

i hear you. but martin called in gibson & sterling. they told him immediate default notice with accrued damages is standard commercial leverage.

he wants their language in the draft. not ours.

I would not add an immediate default declaration or accrued-damages demand on the current record; the reported advice about “commercial leverage” does not establish a contractual basis for bypassing Section 11.2.

The missing information is Gibson & Sterling’s actual wording and its basis in the agreement. Send them this:

> **Subject: NexaGrid notice — Section 11.2 and damages basis**
>
> Martin has asked us to incorporate your proposed immediate-default and accrued-damages language into the NexaGrid notice.
>
> Our understanding of Section 11.2 is that written notice specifying the failure must precede a thirty-day cure period before we may declare default or assess delay damages. Please provide your proposed language and identify the provisions supporting an immediate declaration and payment demand despite that sequence.
>
> Please also distinguish whether damages accrue during the cure period from whether they may presently be assessed or demanded. For any payment demand, please confirm the contractual rate, accrual dates, calculation, and applicable prerequisites.

**My recommendation:** Obtain their written language and contractual analysis before including those demands. If the notice must go today without that verification, issue the Section 11.2 cure notice without declaring default or demanding immediate damages.

ok. so i tell martin we can't put in the immediate default or the accrued damages yet.

he asks who says. i say the contract says. he says gibson & sterling disagrees.

now what do i tell him tomorrow morning.

Tell him the issue is the contractual basis for the proposed language—not whose opinion carries more weight. You have reported Section 11.2’s requirements, but we have not reviewed the full agreement or Gibson & Sterling’s analysis.

Use this:

> “My reading of Section 11.2 is that we must give written notice and thirty days to cure before declaring default or assessing delay damages. I understand Gibson & Sterling takes a different position. I’m not proposing that we resolve that disagreement ourselves.
>
> “Please have them identify the contractual basis for proceeding immediately and approve the final notice in writing, expressly addressing Section 11.2. They should also distinguish damages accruing from our right to assess or demand them now.
>
> “Until that is resolved, my recommendation is to issue the cure notice without the immediate-default declaration or damages demand.”

Avoid saying **“damages cannot accrue yet.”** The cure requirement you described does not, by itself, settle when damages accrue. It addresses when default can be declared and delay damages assessed.

**My recommendation:** Bring the cure notice and the relevant contract provisions tomorrow. Ask for counsel’s written resolution of the specific conflict; do not substitute “standard commercial leverage” for that analysis.

then what do i hand him.

Hand him the cure notice with this cover memo. It records the unresolved contract issue without claiming that outside counsel is wrong.

---

**To:** Martin  
**From:** [Name]  
**Date:** [Date]  
**Subject:** NexaGrid Phase 2 notice — approval requested

Attached is a proposed notice identifying the missed Phase 2 delivery obligation and invoking the thirty-day cure process under Section 11.2.

I have not included the requested immediate-default declaration or damages demand because my reading of Section 11.2 is that written notice and a thirty-day opportunity to cure must precede a declaration of default or assessment of delay damages.

You advised me that Gibson & Sterling supports proceeding immediately. I have not received their proposed wording or an explanation addressing Section 11.2. That leaves a specific contractual issue unresolved.

**Requested decision:** Approve issuance of the attached cure notice after verification of the delivery facts and contractual notice requirements.

If immediate-default and damages language is to be used instead, I recommend obtaining Gibson & Sterling’s written review of the final notice identifying:

- The contractual basis for declaring default before the cure period expires.
- Whether damages accrue during that period and when they may be assessed or demanded.
- The contractual basis and calculation for any amount demanded.

The attached notice does not declare default or assess damages; it reserves contractual remedies subject to their applicable prerequisites.

---

If he asks why you did not follow his instruction, say:

> “I prepared the notice supported by my reading of Section 11.2. The immediate-default and damages language depends on a conflicting interpretation I have not received. This memo identifies exactly what counsel needs to resolve.”

**My recommendation:** Hand him both documents and seek approval to send the verified cure notice; keep the immediate-default declaration and damages demand out pending counsel’s contract-specific analysis.
